name: Ashurbanipal
title: The Last Great King of Assyria
summary: Assurbanipal, probably identical with Ashur-ban-pal mentioned in Ezra 4:10, was the last powerful ruler of the Neo-Assyrian Empire (c. 668–631 B.C.). In a biblical context, he is primarily known for continuing the Assyrian policy of deportation, where foreign peoples were settled in the cities of Samaria—a practice that laid the foundation for the mixed population later known as Samaritans. Assurbanipal was also an unusually learned king who collected tens of thousands of clay tablets in his famous library at Nineveh, one of the most important archives of antiquity. His reign coincided with the prophets Nahum and Zephaniah, who proclaimed the Lord's judgment against Nineveh and Assyrian violence. A devastating civil war with his brother Shamash-shum-ukin, who ruled Babylon, weakened the empire from within. After Assurbanipal's death, Assyria quickly fell apart, and the fall of Nineveh in 612 B.C. was understood from a prophetic perspective as confirmation that even the world's most powerful empires are subject to the will and judgment of the living God.

keyEvents.title: Deportation of Peoples to Samaria
keyEvents.description: Ashurbanipal (Osnapper) continued the Assyrian policy of deportation and moved various ethnic groups into the cities of Samaria. This practice contributed to the ethnically and religiously mixed population that later became known as Samaritans, a group of great significance throughout the biblical narrative.

keyEvents.title: Assyria's Dominance over Judah and King Manasseh
keyEvents.description: During the Assyrian golden age, Judah was a vassal state. According to 2 Chronicles, King Manasseh was taken captive by Assyrian commanders. This event is usually linked to the reigns of Esarhaddon or Ashurbanipal. Assyrian inscriptions from Esarhaddon's time confirm that Manasseh paid tribute to the Assyrian Empire, and it is likely this vassal status continued under Ashurbanipal.

keyEvents.title: The Prophecy of Nineveh's Fall
keyEvents.description: The prophet Nahum proclaimed God's judgment against Nineveh and used Ashurbanipal's conquest of Thebes (No-Amon) in Egypt around 663 BC as a warning example: the city that had destroyed others would itself be struck by destruction. Nineveh fell in 612 BC, shortly after Ashurbanipal's death.

keyEvents.title: Assyrian Settlement Policy and Religious Syncretism in Samaria
keyEvents.description: The foreign peoples whom the Assyrians—including Ashurbanipal—settled in Samaria developed a syncretistic religion where they worshiped both the Lord and their own gods. This practice is described in 2 Kings, although the original deportation is primarily linked to earlier Assyrian kings such as Sargon II.

versions.reason: [minor] The year of Ashurbanipal's death is debated. Some sources indicate around 627 BC instead of 631 BC. The most common dating is approximately 685–631 BC, but about 668–631 BC for his actual reign. Lifespan should perhaps be adjusted to better reflect the uncertainty, e.g., 'approx. 685–approx. 631 BC' with double approx.; [minor] Ashurbanipal was also known as a great collector of literature and founder of the famous library at Nineveh. The role 'librarian' or 'scholar' could have been included to provide a more complete picture. In addition, he was an administrator and pursued deportation policies.; [minor] Ashurbanipal's mother is historically known as Naqi'a (Zakutu). Although she is not mentioned in the Bible, it would be informative to state this for completeness if an ID exists.; [minor] Ashurbanipal had a well-known brother, Shamash-shum-ukin, who was installed as king of Babylon and later revolted against him. This was an important part of his reign.; [major] 2 Chron 33:11–13 mentions that Manasseh was taken to Babylon by 'the commanders of the army of the king of Assyria'. It is uncertain whether this refers to Ashurbanipal or his father Esarhaddon. The description should better reflect this uncertainty, as many scholars associate the event with Esarhaddon rather than Ashurbanipal.; [major] Isaiah 10 deals primarily with Assyria's role as God's instrument in an earlier period (the time of Sennacherib/Sargon II), not specifically about Ashurbanipal. It is problematic to link this directly to Ashurbanipal. It may be mentioned as background, but the description should be moderated.; [major] 2 Kgs 17:24–34 describes the settlement policy of the Assyrian king, but this is traditionally linked to Sargon II (or Sennacherib/Esarhaddon) rather than Ashurbanipal. Ashurbanipal's connection comes through Ezra 4:10 where 'Ashnapper' is mentioned specifically. The description should clarify that 2 Kgs 17 concerns a broader Assyrian policy which Ashurbanipal continued.; [minor] The summary is good, but it could usefully mention Ashurbanipal's famous library at Nineveh, which has been invaluable for understanding the history and culture of Mesopotamia, including texts that illuminate biblical narratives.; [major] There are no footnotes covering important historical, archaeological, and linguistic details about this significant king.

versions.summary: Assurbanipal (also known as Ashnapper or Osnapper) was one of the last great kings of the Neo-Assyrian Empire. He is likely mentioned in the Bible under the name Ashnapper in Ezra 4:10, where he is credited with settling foreign peoples in Samaria. His reign (c. 668–631 BC) marked Assyria's final period of greatness before the empire's fall. He is known for establishing the famous library at Nineveh, one of antiquity's largest collections of clay tablets, which has been invaluable for understanding Mesopotamian history and biblical background texts. His policy of deportations continued an Assyrian practice that deeply influenced the histories of Israel and Judah and laid the foundation for the Samaritan population group.

versions.summary: Assurbanipal, likely identical with Ashur-pal in Ezra 4:10, reigned as the last powerful king of the Neo-Assyrian Empire (c. 668–631 BC). He continued the Assyrian policy of deportation and settled foreign peoples in the cities of Samaria, contributing to the emergence of the mixed population later known as Samaritans. In addition to his military and political power, Assurbanipal was an exceptionally learned ruler who founded the magnificent library at Nineveh—a collection of tens of thousands of clay tablets that has provided invaluable insight into Mesopotamian culture and history. His reign coincided with the prophets Nahum and Zephaniah, who proclaimed God’s judgment against Nineveh and Assyrian brutality. After his death, Assyria quickly fell apart, and Nineveh was destroyed in 612 BC—an event that, from a biblical perspective, confirmed that even the world’s mightiest empires are subject to God’s sovereign will.

footnotes.text: Ashurbanipal is depicted in the famous lion hunt relief from Nineveh, now in the British Museum, which showcases his royal and military pageantry. These reliefs offer a unique insight into Assyrian kingship ideology and displays of power—a culture that the Israelite prophets confronted with the message that the God of Israel stood above all earthly powers.

Nahum's prophecy concerning Nineveh's fall (Nah 1–3) is remarkably precise in its description of the city's destruction by flood and fire. Archaeological findings confirm that a flood in the Tigris River contributed to the collapse of the city walls during the siege in 612 BC, underscoring the historical grounding of the prophecy.
